source_refs.note: Topic 11.2.4 with Quick Check 11.2, printed page 251.

items: Alkanes containing upto four carbon atoms are colourless, odourless, gases while pentane to heptadecane (C₅ to C₁₇) are colourless, odourless liquids. The higher members from C₁₈ onwards are waxy solids which are also colourless and odourless.
Alkanes are non-polar or very weakly polar and are insoluble in polar solvents like water, but soluble in non-polar solvents, such as hexane, benzene, ether, etc.

Their physical constants, e.g. boiling points, melting points, density, etc increase with the increase in number of carbon atoms, whereas solubility decreases with the increase in molecular mass. The boiling points of alkanes having branched chain structures are lower than their isomeric normal chain alkanes, e.g. straight change butane has a higher boiling point -0.50 ºC than 2-Methylpropane (isobutane, -11.7 °C).

blocks.prompt: a) Why do branched alkanes have lower boiling points than the straight-chain alkanes?
blocks.explanation: Alkane molecules are held together only by weak intermolecular forces, and these depend on how much surface the molecules can touch. A straight chain can lie along its whole length against neighbouring molecules. A branched isomer is more compact and rounded and touches less surface, so the forces are weaker and less energy is needed to boil it.

blocks.prompt: b) Explain why alkanes have a tetrahedral shape.
blocks.explanation: Each carbon atom in an alkane is sp³ hybridized: it is surrounded by four bonding electron pairs and no lone pair. The four pairs repel one another equally and move as far apart as possible, at 109.5°; this is the tetrahedral shape.

blocks.prompt: c) Draw the shapes of cyclopropane and cyclopentane.
blocks.explanation: Cyclopropane is a triangular ring of three CH₂ groups (C–C–C angle 60°) and cyclopentane is a pentagonal ring of five CH₂ groups (angle about 108°), as drawn.

answer_figure.alt: Three-part answer diagram: (a) the tetrahedral carbon of methane with four H atoms, one wedge and one dashed bond, H-C-H angle 109.5 degrees; (b) cyclopropane C3H6, a triangular ring of three CH2 groups, angle 60 degrees; (c) cyclopentane C5H10, a pentagonal ring of five CH2 groups, angle about 108 degrees.
answer_figure.caption: Answer diagram: the tetrahedral shape of an alkane carbon, the triangular ring of cyclopropane (C₃H₆) and the pentagonal ring of cyclopentane (C₅H₁₀). (The book's Table 11.5 prints the formula of cyclopentane as C₄H₁₀; the correct formula is C₅H₁₀.)
answer_figure.long_description: The first part shows one carbon atom of an alkane with four bonds to four H atoms: two in the plane of the paper, one thick wedge (towards the viewer) and one dashed line (away from the viewer). The 109.5° angle between two bonds is marked. The second part shows cyclopropane: three CH₂ groups at the corners of a triangle, each C–C–C angle 60°. The third part shows cyclopentane: five CH₂ groups at the corners of a pentagon, angle about 108°.
